title: No One Is Focused on the Middle
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer closes her month-long series on leadership by arguing that the missing piece in large system failures is the connective middle. Using the stalled recovery from the Los Angeles fires, and a letter from Fire Fellows to Spokane after its August fires, she shows how well-intentioned agencies, funders, utilities and survivors can each act reasonably while the whole falls short. She uses an orchestra metaphor in which every section plays but no one is conducting, so music becomes noise. Her point is that leadership attention usually goes to the top (who decides) and the edges (individual voices), while no one tends the space between them. She names five lessons the Fellows believe communities should not have to learn mid-crisis and calls for structures where people who experience, influence, operate and fund a system can build shared understanding. The essay ends with reflection questions and a plug for her book Citizen Leader.
points: Schafer's core claim is that systems fail not from bad faith but because no one is responsible for the connective middle between decision-makers and the people living with the results.
The orchestra image clarifies the missing role as a conductor who hears the whole and holds tempo, not a boss who controls every instrument.
Individual leadership development is necessary but insufficient, since capacity must become collective through structures that connect people across vantage points.
The Fire Fellows' lessons, such as making key agreements in ordinary time and sustaining the caregivers, offer a concrete checklist for any large collaborative effort.
Rebuilding systems exactly as they were is framed as rehearsal for the next failure, which challenges leaders to ask what vulnerabilities they are recreating.
quotes: The whole is still less than the sum of all these reasonable parts. And nearly two years into this work, I increasingly understand why. No one is focused on the middle.

It means the systems that existed before the fire were never designed to carry what a catastrophe of this scale requires. Rebuilding those systems exactly as they were is not recovery. It is rehearsal for the next failure.

Without that capacity, the orchestra does not go silent. Everyone keeps playing. They simply play according to their own score, timeline, incentives and responsibilities until it becomes difficult to distinguish music from noise.
It is not enough for more people to recognize their leadership if all of that leadership remains disconnected. Individual capacity has to become collective capacity.
Without that middle, a teenager’s documentary, a survivor’s op-ed, an elected official’s frustration and a funder’s concern can all be true and still remain scattered.
Not because everyone will agree. Not because everyone gets everything they want. But because there is no sustainable version of one part of a system thriving indefinitely at the expense of another.
perhaps the next evolution is not simply awakening more individual leaders. It is building places where all of that human capacity can meet.
